The Flaky Test Was Right

A workplace chat about the dangerous meaning of “flaky.” An inconsistent test is not automatically a useless test—and a green rerun does not erase the failure you never understood.

#softwaretesting #flakytests #engineering #workplace #developer

Your test passed yesterday. Today it failed. You didn’t touch the code.
That’s not a bug in your app — it’s a flaky test, and it’s more common than you think.
25% of CI failures aren’t real bugs. Even Google sees this on 16% of their own tests.
Most engineers click “re-run” and move on. That’s not a fix — it’s a test that got lucky the second time.
Here’s the real breakdown: 45% race conditions, 20% shared data, 12% test order. Each one has an actual fix.
Save this. You’ll need it the next time your CI goes red for no reason. 👇

Your flaky tests aren't a nuisance - they're a $120,000/year line item.

QA burns 40% of its week maintaining tests that pass one run and fail the next. Here's the real cost.

New data: for a 20-engineer team, flaky tests cost roughly $120K/year in wasted time - and 77% of developers say flaky tests directly steal time from shipping. The tests, not the code, become the bottleneck.

The hidden tax is maintenance. Around 40% of a QA team's week goes to re-running, quarantining, and debugging tests that break for no real reason. That's not testing - that's babysitting.

Here's what most teams miss: a flaky test is worse than no test. It trains everyone to ignore red. So the day a real bug finally turns the suite red, nobody believes it.

The fix isn't "write more tests." It's stability - isolate the flakiness, quarantine and fix the root cause, and treat test reliability as a first-class metric you actually measure.

How much of your team's week disappears into flaky-test maintenance - and is anyone even measuring it?
